title: Rafael and the Well
premise: Folklorist Rosalind Dravenmoor returns to the decaying family house in Hollowmere to record the village's forbidden songs, only to find the mirrors lagging a second behind reality—and in that lagged reflection, a figure standing in the old well house. Digging through their grandmother's papers, Rosalind learns that in 1974 the Dravenmoors sealed a wronged woman, Maren Oduya, alive in the well to claim her land and her voice, and the family's quiet power has been fed by that theft ever since. As the well begins to refill and the lag widens, Rosalind must choose between the inheritance that kept them safe and invisible, and a justice the law will never deliver. They open the well, give Maren back her name and her songs, and let the house—and their claim to it—collapse into the water, escaping with nothing but a recording that finally sings true.
about_author: Jonah Quintana is the pen name of a former archivist who spent a decade cataloguing estate sales and unclaimed inheritances, an experience that left him suspicious of every family that keeps its records locked. He writes horror from a farmhouse in upstate New York, where the well water, he insists, tastes fine.

chapters.title: Songs You Don't Sing Twice
chapters.summary: Rosalind's POV. Arriving at Hollowmere to record the village's half-silenced ballads, Rosalind notices every singer stops mid-verse when the well house comes into view. An old woman, Edith, sings one line twice by accident and crosses herself. The emotional beat is unease disguised as academic curiosity—the reader senses the village knows something Rosalind doesn't.

chapters.title: One Second Behind
chapters.summary: Rosalind's POV. In the darkened house, Rosalind catches the hallway mirror showing a door closing a beat after it actually closes. Testing every mirror, they confirm the lag—and in the lagged reflection of the hall, a figure stands at the window that no one is at yet. The beat is creeping dread: the house is not delayed, it is rehearsing.

chapters.title: The Grandmother's Ledger
chapters.summary: Rosalind's POV, with interleaved 1974 ledger entries. In the locked study, Rosalind finds accounts of land purchases from Maren Oduya, a Black folk singer whose ballads the Dravenmoors copyrighted under their own name. The final entry, dated the night of the autumn equinox 1974, simply reads: 'Well secured. Voice secured.' The beat is horrified recognition of family as predator.

chapters.title: What the Village Gave Up
chapters.summary: Rosalind interviews Edith and the pub landlord, whose POVs surface in recorded testimony. They describe Maren: the songs she sang, the night she went to the well house to reclaim her deed, and how the Dravenmoors 'settled it quiet.' The village prospered and stopped singing. The beat is complicity—the whole community chose comfort over justice.

chapters.title: The Lag Widens
chapters.summary: Rosalind's POV. The mirror delay stretches to three seconds, then five; Rosalind watches their reflected self hesitate before moving, then move before being told to. Water stains bloom on the study ceiling in the shape of a mouth. The beat is loss of control—the house is no longer showing Rosalind the future; it's making offers.

chapters.title: The Inheritance
chapters.summary: Rosalind's POV, with a letter from the grandmother. A solicitor's letter confirms the estate passes to Rosalind on condition the well house remain sealed—seventeen previous heirs signed the same clause; their names are all crossed out in the ledger. The grandmother's letter warns: 'It only asks for one thing. Never give it your voice.' The beat is temptation with teeth.

chapters.title: Maren's Verse
chapters.summary: Alternating Rosalind's POV and the lagged reflection's POV. In the mirror-world, Rosalind finally hears the missing verses of Maren's ballad sung from the well house, describing exactly how she died. Rosalind realizes the lag isn't a haunting—it's Maren, still waiting one second behind the world, asking to be brought forward. The beat is terrible empathy.

chapters.title: The Offer
chapters.summary: Rosalind's POV. The house manifests its bargain: the lagged reflection shows Rosalind a life of safety, wealth, and perfect invisibility—everything they've wanted—if they sign the new clause and stay quiet. The mirrors fill with the crossed-out names of heirs who refused. The beat is the corrupting sweetness of power, and Rosalind's near-surrender.

chapters.title: Equinox, Rising Water
chapters.summary: Rosalind's POV, climax. On the equinox the well refills; the house floods upward from below, and the mirrors show Maren's face over Rosalind's own. Rosalind breaks the seal, descends into the well house, speaks Maren's name and her stolen verses aloud into the rising water—returning the voice—and the mirrors shatter in sequence like a held breath released. The beat is sacrifice and reckoning.

chapters.title: The Recording That Sings True
chapters.summary: Rosalind's POV, coda. The house has collapsed into the well; Rosalind walks away with one tape and no inheritance. In Hollowmere, Edith sings Maren's ballad complete, twice, and nothing happens. The final mirror fragment in Rosalind's bag reflects in perfect real time—except once, at dusk, a hand seems to wave. The beat is justice delivered outside the law, and peace that costs everything.
